title: Chapter 24. Of the Nutrition, and Procreation of a Commonwealth
paragraphs: The NUTRITION of a commonwealth consists in the plenty and distribution of the materials that sustain life; in their concoction, or preparation; and (once prepared) in their conveyance, by suitable conduits, to public use.

As for the plenty of matter, it is a thing limited by nature to those commodities which God, from the two breasts of our common mother — land and sea — either gives freely to mankind or sells to it for labour.

For the matter of this nourishment, consisting in animals, vegetables, and minerals, God has laid them freely before us, on or near the face of the earth; so that nothing more is needed than the labour and industry of gathering them in. Plenty therefore depends (next to God's favour) simply on the labour and industry of men.

This matter, commonly called commodities, is partly native and partly foreign — native being what is to be had within the territory of the commonwealth, foreign being what is imported from outside. And because there is no territory under the dominion of one commonwealth (except one of very vast extent) that produces all things needful for the maintenance and motion of the whole body, and few that do not produce something more than necessary, the surplus commodities within can cease to be surplus by being used to supply needs at home, in return for things to be had abroad — whether by exchange, by just war, or by labour. For a man's labour is also a commodity, exchangeable for benefit as much as anything else. And there have been commonwealths which, with no more territory than served them for habitation, have nevertheless not only maintained but also increased their power, partly by the labour of trading from one place to another, and partly by selling manufactures whose raw materials were brought in from other places.

The distribution of the materials of this nourishment is the constitution of mine, thine, and his — in one word, property; and in every kind of commonwealth it belongs to the sovereign power. For where there is no commonwealth, there is (as has already been shown) a perpetual war of every man against his neighbour; so everything is his who can get it and keep it by force — which is neither property nor community, but uncertainty. This is so evident that even Cicero (a passionate defender of liberty), in a public pleading, attributes all property to the civil law: 'Let the civil law,' he says, 'be once abandoned, or even negligently guarded — not to say oppressed — and there is nothing that any man can be sure to receive from his ancestor, or to leave to his children.' And again: 'Take away the civil law, and no man knows what is his own and what is another's.' Since therefore the introduction of property is an effect of the commonwealth, which can do nothing except by the person who represents it, it is the act of the sovereign alone; and it consists in the laws, which none can make who do not have the sovereign power. The ancients knew this well, calling Nomos (that is, distribution) what we call law, and defining justice as distributing to each man his own.
All private estates of land proceed originally from the arbitrary distribution of the sovereign.

In this distribution, the first law is for the division of the land itself, in which the sovereign assigns to each man a portion according as he — and not as any subject, or any number of subjects — shall judge agreeable to equity and the common good. The children of Israel were a commonwealth in the wilderness, but lacked the commodities of the earth until they were masters of the Land of Promise; which was afterwards divided among them, not by their own discretion but by the discretion of Eleazar the priest and Joshua their general. When there were twelve tribes, made thirteen by the subdivision of the tribe of Joseph, they nevertheless made only twelve portions of the land, and assigned no land to the tribe of Levi, giving them instead the tenth part of all the fruits. So that division was therefore arbitrary. And though a people coming into possession of a land by war does not always exterminate the ancient inhabitants (as the Jews did), but leaves many, most, or all of them their estates, it is plain they afterwards hold those estates from the victor's distribution — as the people of England held all theirs from William the Conqueror.
A subject's property does not exclude the dominion of the sovereign, but only that of another subject.

From which we may gather that the property a subject has in his lands consists in the right to exclude all other subjects from the use of them, and not in the right to exclude his sovereign, whether an assembly or a monarch. For since the sovereign — that is, the commonwealth (whose person he represents) — is understood to do nothing except in order to the common peace and security, this distribution of lands is to be understood as done in order to the same. Consequently, whatever distribution he makes to the prejudice of that end is contrary to the will of every subject, who committed his peace and safety to the sovereign's discretion and conscience; and by the will of every one of them, it is to be reputed void. It is true that a sovereign monarch, or the greater part of a sovereign assembly, may ordain the doing of many things in pursuit of their passions, contrary to their own consciences — which is a breach of trust, and of the law of nature; but this is not enough to authorise any subject either to make war on, or so much as to accuse of injustice, or in any way to speak evil of, their sovereign. Because they have authorised all his actions, and in bestowing the sovereign power, made them their own. But in what cases the commands of sovereigns are contrary to equity and the law of nature is to be considered later in another place.

In the distribution of land, the commonwealth itself may be conceived to have a portion, possessing and improving it through its representative; and such a portion may be made sufficient to cover the whole expense of the common peace and defence that is necessarily required. Which would be very true if any representative could be conceived free from human passions and infirmities. But the nature of men being what it is, setting aside public land, or any fixed revenue, for the commonwealth is futile, and tends to the dissolution of government — and to the condition of mere nature, and war — as soon as ever the sovereign power falls into the hands of a monarch, or assembly, that is either too careless of money or too willing to risk the public stock in a long or costly war. Commonwealths can endure no diet: for since their expense is not limited by their own appetite, but by external accidents and the appetites of their neighbours, the public riches cannot be limited by any other bounds than what the emerging occasions shall require. And whereas in England the Conqueror reserved various lands to his own use (besides forests and chases, either for his recreation or for the preservation of woods), and various services on the land he gave his subjects, it seems these were not reserved for his maintenance in his public capacity but in his natural capacity: for he and his successors, even so, laid arbitrary taxes on all subjects' land when they judged it necessary. Or if those public lands and services were ordained as a sufficient maintenance for the commonwealth, that was contrary to the scope of the institution; being (as the ensuing taxes showed) insufficient, and (as appears from the recent revenue of the Crown) subject to alienation and diminution. It is therefore vain to assign a portion to the commonwealth, which may sell or give it away — and does sell, and does give it away, when this is done by its representative.

As with the distribution of lands at home, so also to assign in what places, and for what commodities, subjects shall trade abroad belongs to the sovereign. For if it belonged to private persons to use their own discretion in this, some of them would, for the sake of gain, be drawn both to supply the enemy with means of harming the commonwealth, and to harm it themselves by importing things that, however pleasing to men's appetites, are nevertheless harmful or at least unprofitable to them. So it belongs to the commonwealth (that is, to the sovereign alone) to approve or disapprove of both the places and the matter of foreign trade.

Further, since for the sustenance of a commonwealth it is not enough that every man have property in a portion of land, or in some few commodities, or a natural ability in some useful art — and since there is hardly any art in the world that is not necessary either to the being or to the well-being of almost every particular man — it is necessary that men distribute what they can spare, and transfer their property in it, one to another, by exchange and mutual contract. So it belongs to the commonwealth (that is, to the sovereign) to appoint in what manner all kinds of contract between subjects — buying, selling, exchanging, borrowing, lending, letting, and hiring — are to be made, and by what words and signs they shall be taken to be valid. And concerning the matter and distribution of nourishment to the various members of the commonwealth, this much (considering the scale of the whole work) is sufficient.

By concoction I mean the reducing of all commodities that are not at present consumed, but reserved for nourishment in time to come, to something of equal value, and so portable that it does not hinder the motion of men from place to place; so that a man may have, in whatever place he may be, such nourishment as the place affords. And this is nothing but gold, silver, and money. For gold and silver, being (as it happens) highly valued in almost all countries of the world, are a convenient measure of the value of all other things between nations; and money (of whatever material, coined by the sovereign of a commonwealth) is a sufficient measure of the value of all other things between the subjects of that commonwealth. By means of these measures, all commodities, movable and immovable, are made to accompany a man to every place he visits, within and outside the place of his ordinary residence; and money passes from man to man within the commonwealth, going round and nourishing (as it passes) every part of it. So this concoction is, as it were, the sanguification of the commonwealth: for natural blood is in the same way made from the fruits of the earth, and circulating, nourishes on the way every member of the body of man.

And because silver and gold get their value from the material itself, they have first this advantage: that their value cannot be altered by the power of one, or of a few, commonwealths, being a common measure of the commodities of all places. But base money may easily be raised or debased. Second, they have the advantage of enabling commonwealths to move, and to stretch out their arms in case of need into foreign countries, supplying not only private subjects who travel, but also whole armies with provisions. But a coin that is significant not for its material, but for the stamp of the place that issued it, being unable to endure a change of air, has its effect only at home — where also it is subject to changes of laws, and so to having its value diminished, often to the prejudice of those who hold it.

The conduits and ways by which money is conveyed to public use are of two sorts. One conveys it into the public coffers; the other issues it out again for public payments. Of the first sort are collectors, receivers, and treasurers; of the second are the treasurers again, and the officers appointed for paying the various public or private ministers. And in this too the artificial man keeps his resemblance with the natural; whose veins, receiving the blood from the various parts of the body, carry it to the heart, where, being made vital, the heart sends it out again through the arteries to enliven and to set in motion all the members of the same.

The procreation, or children, of a commonwealth are what we call plantations, or colonies: numbers of men sent out from the commonwealth, under a leader or governor, to inhabit a foreign country, either previously empty of inhabitants, or emptied at the time by war. And when a colony is settled, the colonists are either a commonwealth of their own, discharged from subjection to the sovereign who sent them (as has been done by many commonwealths of ancient time) — in which case the commonwealth they came from was called their metropolis, or mother, and requires no more of them than fathers require of the children they emancipate and free from their domestic government: namely, honour and friendship — or else they remain united to their metropolis, as were the colonies of the people of Rome; and then they are not commonwealths themselves but provinces, and parts of the commonwealth that sent them. So the rights of colonies (saving honour, and league with their metropolis) depend wholly on the licence, or letters, by which their sovereign authorised them to plant.
